Well, for the original trilogy it's kind of a standard hero's journey, but I think that's partly only because so many people copied it because it was good and it became standard. You've got the big Galactic Empire that controls most of the galaxy and the small but well-formed Rebel Alliance that relies on guerilla tactics to disrupt the Empire and try and bring it down slowly. The series mostly follows Luke Skywalker, a guy from a backwater desert planet that farms moisture out of the air and ground (because desert), who gets swept up in major galactic events that he has no clue about and finds that he's more important than anybody actually could have known. Over the series he goes from a young man with fantastical dreams of escapism to a mature warrior, grounded in reality. There are other major characters, but he's the real focus throughout the trilogy. All of this is taking place in a vast universe with so much going on, and almost everything you see has a backstory if you're willing to search for it. There's so much that's unknown and alien at first, and the more I learn about it the more I love it. But I digress.

Star Wars is basically the source of a ton of common tropes in fiction, and probably the best example of most of them. If you're looking for a great sci-fi/fantasy with a great story and absolutely fantastic worldbuilding, this is the one.

That would be the EU. The Expanded Universe is what happened when a bunch of authors basically decided that Star Wars was amazing and they wanted more, and George Lucas kind of gave them an "all right, whatever". They took the universe and ran with it. The timeline of Star Wars now goes from over a hundred thousand years before Ep1 to several hundred after Ep6. There's also an "official" book for each movie, which goes over everything the movie does and also adds clarifications, fixes inconsistencies, and builds the world some more. I'd still highly recommend watching the movies, though, even if you're not that big of a movie person. Star Wars is one of those series that everybody should see at least once. I've heard of people not liking them a whole lot, but I've never heard of someone hating them or even actively disliking them.

Modern governments are not foolish enough to try, and shape the culture to the extent they did in Farenheit 451. But they have no problems hiding, or destroying specific information that the general public is now aware about, and if anyone tries to hinder or undermine them they will throw them into prison under laws that serve no purpose other than to keep certain people in power.

Think Bradley (Chelsea) Manning, or Edward Snowden. Manning got 30 years for releasing information, and they are drooling to arrest Snowden. Had Snowden become a public figure they would've probably assassinated him.

The thing is, they don't really NEED to censor books. People don't seem to read as much as they used to, opting for visual media instead. I'm not arguing that any medium for storytelling is superior to another, but it's an unavoidable fact that there are an astonishing number of people out there-- intelligent, educated people-- who simply do not read for recreation. If the government is at all concerned with censoring the arts, I would think they'd focus their efforts on film and television instead.

Please note that I have no idea to what extent the US government really cares about censoring free speech in the arts. I would think they'd be more concerned about censoring facts in nonfiction works, than censoring themes or ideologies in fiction.
